comments.text:
​ @lizardx6504  
No.
It’s true that on NVIDIA a new driver could compromise stability across different graphics cards, but this happens very rarely with AMD because the two architectures are conceptually very different.
With NVIDIA’s architecture, you have to optimize card by card.
Change the compilation of a shader? You’ll need to check if it works in various situations on all GPUs, because changes often affect VRAM usage and allocation. And since NVIDIA has always played badly with planned obsolescence by forcing VRAM capacity (the latest generation gives clear examples!), this often means that a tweak for the 5080 crashes all cards that don’t have 16 GB of VRAM.
Remember Indiana Jones where a 4080 outperformed a 5080 because the 5080 hit VRAM saturation over just 400 MB?
Exactly that—even though in that case, besides drivers, they had to patch the game to make some background textures lighter, or those 400 MB couldn’t be removed.
(If you’re curious, the 400 MB were due to the different logical addressing structure of compute units between the 4080 and 5080.)
On AMD, you have unified VRAM, and AMD never forced VRAM quantity like NVIDIA did, so changes usually work across all cards.
This is also why AMD drivers are called “Fine Wine”: a shader compilation change applies across the entire architecture from HD 7000 to Vega, from RDNA1 to RDNA4 (I separated them because those are two distinct ISAs: one GCN and one RDNA).
When things improved with Polaris, the improvement reflected all the way back to HD 7000, the first GCN cards.
So on this point, I need to correct you to clarify your ideas.
And don’t worry it’s perfectly normal for some people to pound the table indignantly… it’s marketing.
They have their reasons to write falsehoods about AMD—maybe hoping to earn an extra dollar on stocks, or they’re directly involved in NVIDIA GPU sales (which aren’t selling right now, and that’s also why some sites are defaming AMD, paid, of course).
If you know how it works, you know that every now and then NVIDIA triggers an unjustified shitstorm against AMD (one might say unjustified because NVIDIA’s sales are huge, but the truth is NVIDIA sells 80% of its products to just 5 OEMs for laptops; the truth no one wants to admit is that in gaming, with desktop gaming GPUs, not laptops, AMD sells more).
And you also know there will be fanatics and opportunists pushing certain “non-truths,” but things will keep working as always.
Remember when Igor tested the RX 480 and said it would burn all enthusiasts’ motherboards because of its extremely high power draw?
Not a single one burned, not even years later.
There was just one guy who tried to pass off his broken motherboard as caused by his new RX 480, but the clumsy screwdriver scratches cutting PCIe lines while removing the old GPU were obvious… what can you do? There’s always someone who tries.

comments.text:
The advantage of Geforce in games is ray tracing. Many people think that they can just turn off ray tracing, but more and more recent games are forcing you to use light ray tracing. Even if you turn it off in the settings, you cannot turn it off completely. It is designed as a game for GeForce, and it is intentionally designed to give GeForce an advantage. 
Looking at the graph in this video, any smart person will have noticed that although the 9070XT is clearly inferior to the 5070Ti in average FPS, the difference is small at 1% Low. I think this is because Geforce is energy efficient, while Radeon always runs at maximum power consumption. In other words, the Radeon's high power consumption is not a waste at all, but is beneficial in the actual gaming experience. Also, it should not be ignored that the 9070XT is not significantly inferior, even when including games developed for Geforce, which force a little ray tracing. If we look at truly pure rasterization performance and 1% Low, this generation of Radeon is more than able to compete on equal terms with Geforce. The balance of power will change dramatically once SUPER is released, but the price will also change significantly, so make sure you consider what suits your needs and budget before buying. I like both green and red, and I respect the opinion of those who like DLSS because it blows FSR away in performance and compatibility. This time I bought the Red Devil 9070XT, but since Radeon doesn't have RTX VSR, I might buy a Geforce next. If the power consumption of my next GPU exceeds 300W, I would like to avoid 16-pin if possible.

Honestly the 9070 with an oc and power budget to match the 9070xt comes so close in performance, its just another generation of amd having its GPU cores bottlenecked by anemic memory bandwidth. Cards that share the same memory config and had very similar performance when core speeds are the same despite different core counts:
290(x)

470/480
Vega (56/64)
5700(xt)
6800xt/6900xt

comments.text:
@joefield5217  To be fair, the support pull has been VASTLY exaggerated, mostly by people being modern...a.k.a. shout like a monkey and verify after. 

I don't have any certainty that your 9070XT might be obsolete in 3 years or 10 years...but neither do I for any GeForce GPU...not with all the shenanigans going on with upscaling, AI and other crap that's being focused on today instead of games being well optimized as to not require those tricks. 

I know from past experience though...that my R9 380 in my father's PC can still play games, but of course the performance for modern titles is nonexistent.
My RX 580 still runs without complaints in my sister's PC, my current 7800XT runs great and I'm sure the 9070XT that I'm getting next week is also gonna run for years to come. 

I've heard similar experiences with GeForce GPUs, only complaints have been in VRAM limited cards that could squeeze more FPS, but were held back by the memory buffer. 

Technology advances really fast...you can see that FSR4 FP8 for example requires some hardware that previous cards, even my 7800XT doesn't have...this isn't a "ahahahha fuck you customer"...it's the natural progression of tech. 
I appreciate that there's also an FSR4 Int8 model being worked on that is shaping up to be decent, but then again...I bought the card for FPS not gimmicks. 

We should turn our gaze and pressure towards game developers who have become lazy and complacent...making half assed games, that run like crap all because they crutch on the upscalers to salvage the performance. 

For example, Battlefield 6 has to be commended. To have 100FPS natively at 1440p with the settings cranked to the max and the visual quality that game has for a xx70 tier card is good. 
Most recent trash that Tim tested though barely gets 60, Borderlands 4 being an egregious example of trash optimization by the game devs.

So, what I'm trying to say is...keep your 9070XT, play your games...if you encounter deal breaker issues like games not even launching down the line...change it then, but don't dwell on things that MIGHT affect you in the future. 
We don't know what the future holds...we can speculate, but I wouldn't base a financial decision on speculation.

comments.text:
@nicane-9966  So, from a pure technical standpoint, yes, he is wrong, because "No more driver update[s]" doesn't even apply to the "worst case" maintenance mode. Maintenance mode always includes bug fixes and security updates as required.

But from a more contextual standpoint ... he's also wrong.
Mainly because either statement of AMD doesn't say something the other doesn't. People just got overly hung up on "focus/concentrate" and interpreted it in the worst case.
Furthermore, the actual impact of RDNA 2 going into maintenance mode isn't something we can even know right now, and it's only really something that will become apparent over the next year or so. Keep in mind that driver optimizations are only one side of the story. Since RDNA 2 has been out for 5 years, that gave AMD a long time to work with game studios to optimize the drivers, which is pretty much the main purpose of game specific optimization driver updates. Also, game devs haven't suddenly lost access to the optimization methods already in place, meaning, if the drivers are solid, they pretty much already know everything they have to to get the best out of them.

So, if AMD was correct in their assessment and the RDNA 2 drivers have already been stable for a while, and having them be in active "development" would result in largely diminishing returns, then it doesn't really matter how old RDNA 2 is, since those drivers will, generally speaking, simply perform as expected into the future, and the actual optimization entirely depends on the game developers.
Should AMD have been wrong in their assessment, then the RDNA 2 line will see a decrease in relative performance for upcoming games, but, well, that's simply not something we can know yet.

And before anyone comes at me with "but Nvidia actively supports for much longer", yes, they technically do, but the game specific optimizations for the old cards could be anywhere from actually useful to basically just a line on paper to be technically correct. And the overarching drivers also led to the problem Nvidia has atm, where since the launch of the 50-series pretty much all of their cards are having driver issues. If Nvidia had branched off older cards, then those driver problems could have possibly been contained to the newer lines.

But, yes, so far this entire thing has really just been a future worry at worst, and something with absolutely no impact on RDNA 1/2 cards at best. Ultimately, we just don't know yet.

​ @albert2006xp  
You’ll surely find someone who will give you an exhaustive list, but… no, there are no differences at all.
NVIDIA cards cost more because NVIDIA’s marketing has a higher cost.
This includes the ads you see on websites, but also things people generally don’t want to talk about, like manipulating public opinion through compliant sites and sponsorships in games to insert proprietary tools, which can then be used to make competitors perform worse.
Want a small proof?
NVIDIA makes developers implement FSR (but only up to version 2.1) in the games it sponsors, just to show NVIDIA buyers that DLSS is better than FSR, and it’s been doing this forever.
You have more NVIDIA-sponsored games with FSR than AMD-sponsored games with DLSS, plus NVIDIA sponsors 90% of games.
Basically, we have FSR only because NVIDIA makes it happen.
But how does it make it happen?
See, they’re different algorithms, but they work on the same calculation principles, using the same data.
The biggest difference is that FSR used to be computed only on shaders, which meant higher computational resource usage compared to DLSS, which partly relied on tensor cores.
To fix this, AMD built FSR in FP16, because for how it’s designed, that precision is more than enough—and mainly because an AMD FP32 compute unit can be used as two independent FP16 units, effectively doubling compute power in that specific base.
This performance difference (tensor cores can give a big boost in certain tasks) means that when you upscale with FSR, it can only enlarge by a factor of 1.3x, while DLSS can go up to 1.5x.
Not a big deal, because you start from a higher internal rendering resolution, so you lose fewer details and help the final image quality.
Now imagine NVIDIA cards don’t have the same FP32 compute system as AMD, so if they need to compute in FP16, they’ll still use an FP32 unit, emulating the less precise base. Imagine the data extracted for upscaling is provided with the same scale used for DLSS, which uses 1.5x enlargement for its best quality level, while for FSR that level corresponds to the balanced setting in terms of quality. And imagine that everyone comparing FSR and DLSS uses, for convenience, only an NVIDIA card, because it can run both.
You know what happens?
The NVIDIA buyer tries FSR on their NVIDIA card and sees it performs worse—because they’re using a GPU that doesn’t have FP16 and therefore struggles twice as much to compute FSR. And it looks worse too, because they’re using a ratio that, given the algorithm’s structure, matches DLSS Balanced, not Quality.
The only result you get is DLSS being praised.
That’s why it’s implemented in NVIDIA-sponsored games.
FSR3 won’t be implemented, because it can be directly swapped with FSR4 DLLs, which—unfortunately for NVIDIA—also use tensor cores, and therefore also start from a 1.5x enlargement level.
So if you play an NVIDIA-sponsored game, like Alan Wake 2, where natively a 5070 Ti performs exactly like a 7900 XTX, using DLSS in Quality will give you a certain result and good image reconstruction. If you use FSR on a 5070 Ti, you’ll see worse image quality—similar to DLSS Balanced—while performance is only slightly better. But if you use FSR on a 7900 XTX, image quality doesn’t improve much, but performance is 25% higher than the 5070 Ti.
Starting from identical native performance, using FSR as intended, in FP16, and in a Balanced setting instead of Quality gives you a huge performance surplus, which DLSS can barely match by switching to Balanced too, reaching the same quality as FSR.
Manipulation.
Can NVIDIA do something dishonest like this with FSR?
Yes, because it’s open, so the excuse is that to match performance for its GPUs that don’t use FP16, they’re “forced” to blast FSR quality.
But they’ll never include FSR3, because at that point you could easily swap to FSR4 and use tensor cores, staying at the 1.5x enlargement ratio, which is the maximum quality level for this algorithm, beating NVIDIA’s marketing, because now you have both quality and tensor power using FSR4 on a 9000 series card.
So yes, they can give you any list you want, but the point is that the cards perform the same, and what you pay extra goes to fund these tricks in games.
And unfortunately for NVIDIA, today, to keep up the same impression, it’s forced to sponsor almost all games—or the trick gets exposed… and paying everyone costs a lot.

comments.text:
@Grstrangler  No, to make it very short it is not user error, it's a combination of the connector and power stage design on the Graphics Card side.

I cannot give you links, because of youtube, but I can give you the titles of videos to search for. Just take out the brackets "". 

The first thing is that Igor Wallosek of Igorslab did a material analysis on the 12VHPWR connector and found out that the pins contained too much copper and too little tin, making them to weak and some bent irrepairably after as little as 5 connections. 
This was before the 12V2x6 replacement of the 12VHPWR. 
The Article. 
"Smoldering Headers on NVIDIA’s GeForce RTX 4090 – New Insights, Measurements and (Un)known Causes of the 12VHPWR and 12V-2×6 Issue | Update"

Then Roman "DerB8uer" Hartung made another analysis here of the 5090's connectors melting. 
"12VHPWR on RTX 5090 is Extremely Concerning"

Then Actually Hardcore overclocking (also known as buildzoid) explained the theory behind it, namely that Nvidia went from three power stages that were load balanced, because it was based on a design for the 8-Pin where you needed three cables to pull 450W, on the 3090Ti. 
To two basically 1 power stage for all 6 cables on the 4090 and 5090, becaus while they had 2 shunt resistors controlling it, since they connected all the power wires to a single 12V rail before reaching the shunts. 
So the shunt resistors and the board logic see them as one wire, they cannot see invidividual cables or power wires. 
And to make it even worse on the 5090 Founders Editon, there is only one shunt resistor. 

He then explained how in theory you could cut 5 of the 6 power wires and the card would still work, pulling all the 600W via one cable which would burn. 
While on the 3090Ti  you could have at max 3 power wires (one per power stage) disconnected or cut and it would would still work, pulling 200W per cable, which most of them can still take. 
Now if two power cables per power stage would be disconnected or cut, the 3090Ti  card would not start. 
"How Nvidia made the 12VHPWR connector even worse."

This led Roman to demonstrate this in practice where he cut 4, yes physically cut 4 of the 6 power wires of a connector and demonstrated how the card then still works and how this overloads the two wires. 
He didn't demonstrate cutting the 5th wire, as that was deemed to much of a safety hazard. 
Video
"The real "User Error" is with Nvidia"

And the problem is, the 5090 is the flagship card, everything else is going to have worse power staging, yes less power, decidedly so, but as the Radeons with melting 12V2x6 haven proven, the power draw is not the issue, it's the load balancing. 
And if that ever leads to a recall and the german VDE, which is the independant regulator, is investigating it, it would hurt Nvidia very badly, as it would affect three generations of cards. Very expensive cards at that. And then there would be the damages for the AIBs. 
That's why they push the "User Error" claim so aggressively, so that nobody dares to look at it or face ridicule by anyone.

Actually Hardcore Overclocking then explained why PSU's don't power balance power connectors, for all those saying we need the power-balancing in PSUs.
"Why ATX power supplies don't load-balance power connectors"

Next the Radeons, well Sapphire did the exact same thing as Nvidia....no power balancing on their Nitro+, they have the same weakness as the Nvidias. 
However they have one advantage, they split the giant 12V Power rail into two reasonably sized ones with fuzes, so if it goes bad, at least it doesn't go as catastropically bad. 
"A look at the Sapphire Implementation of the 12VHPWR Connector"

If you still want more info after that (and I'm beat right now) there is this video from Buildzoid/Actually hardcore overclocking
"Rambling about GPU power connector power balancing."

You made another error on the 7900XTX....you went for the Minimum power supply size...you can do that with a very good PSU, but not with a cheap one. And only if you don't exactly run a lot of things in the system. 
Add some extra SSDs, some HDDs, maybe some additional drives, input devices or USB devices off it and you're in big trouble. 
I run the XFX 7900XT which has a minimum required PSU of 700W* and the recommendation for me was 750W or  850W based on my hardware and PSU calculator, and I went "I want more Headroom, especially since this is the XFX RX 7900XT Merc 310 Black Edition OC Model which pulls up to 350/354W" and bought a Corsair HX1000W. I had a Corsair HX750W before. 
You never, ever scrimp on PSUs, I can recommend Be Quiet! and Corsair from personal experience. And I would only recommend from 80+ Silver and up....Gold is fine, Platinum not a necessity, unless you can easily afford it.

There's a PSU Tier list, read up on, check the PSUs how good it is and what weaknesses it has before buying. 
I also did, as always connect two seperate 8-pin Cables instead of doing the one cable with both connectors that a lot of people do. 
Which afaik also puts them on different 12V rails in the PSU. 
And boy was I glad I did, when I caught a 504Watt less than 1 second transient spike with the early drivers in Star Citizen with CapframeX. Didn't happen after 23.7.1, but damn was I glad. 

And that's one of the key problems with all this, the transient spikes which can go very, very high over the usual card power draw. A friend of mine has a 5090 after a 4090, but he also does AI work with them. And he is running a 1200W or 1500W PSU, because he's also running at 14900K and wants some overhead for the transient spikes. The ATX 3.1 specs allow for an excursion of up to 1200W for 1 MS of which the 5090 draws up to 901W for less than 1 MS, and 823.6 W for 1-5 MS. 
More on that in the article on Igors lab
"NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Founders Edition Review – The 600-Watt Powerhouse in Gaming and Lab Tests" page 14. 

*which I thought wildly optimistic. Especially given that the XFX drew in practice up to 349-354W instead of the 300W given by the Techpowerup site.
